prerequisites: Accurate reading of the complete task.
goals: Select and interpret relevant source material without changing its meaning.
Adapt form, tone and register to the required purpose and audience.
Develop and proofread a coherent response.

sections.title: Read the writing task before choosing your approach
paragraphs: Section B asks for one source-based writing response. Identify the audience, purpose and required form before planning: a recommendation to local residents needs different choices from a formal complaint to an organisation. Register is the level and style of language suited to that relationship; tone is the attitude conveyed.

The Issue 4 allocation for Question 8 is 30 marks: 10 for AO1, 12 for AO4 and 8 for AO5. Source selection and interpretation, effective communication, and accuracy all matter. These are official examination allocations, not the site’s custom quiz marks or a fixed number of marks per paragraph.

example.question: An original task asks for a speech to classmates recommending improvements to a study space. What three decisions should guide your plan?
steps: Audience: classmates, who need clear relevant reasons.
Purpose: recommend improvements and explain their value.
Form: speech, with direct address and a coherent spoken argument.
example.explanation: Choose content and presentation to meet the actual task.

commonMistakes: Writing a literary-analysis essay instead of the requested form.
Treating decorative formatting as a substitute for communication.

practice.question: You are asked to write a formal recommendation to local residents about a proposed park event. Identify the audience, purpose and an appropriate register.
practice.answer: Audience: local residents. Purpose: recommend a position about the proposed event. Register: suitably formal and clear, with reasons relevant to residents.
practice.explanation: These choices shape the response. They do not supply the missing source evidence or prescribe a fixed number of paragraphs.

sections.title: Select source ideas that serve the purpose
paragraphs: Read both source texts carefully and choose ideas relevant to the task. Information, perspectives and reasons can all be useful, but not every detail needs to be repeated. Check whether a source states a fact, offers an opinion or describes one particular experience.

Keep essential qualifications. “Some visitors prefer quiet mornings” does not establish that every visitor dislikes an afternoon event. Using a source well means preserving its meaning while deciding how its ideas support the new response.

example.question: Original source A says that evening users need lighting; source B says that daytime users want shaded seating. Select ideas for a proposal to improve a public garden.
steps: Provide suitable lighting for evening access.
Include shaded seating for daytime use.
Connect both to the different users rather than claiming everyone needs the same feature.
example.explanation: The response combines relevant needs without changing either source’s scope.

commonMistakes: Using only a convenient detail from one source when both are needed.
Changing a qualified claim into a universal fact.

practice.question: A hypothetical source says, “Some visitors prefer quiet mornings.” Explain why changing this to “Every visitor dislikes afternoon events” misuses the source.
practice.answer: It changes some visitors into every visitor and replaces a preference for quiet mornings with opposition to afternoon events. Neither stronger claim is established by the given sentence.
practice.explanation: Preserve both the scope of a claim and what it actually says when selecting and adapting source ideas.

sections.title: Develop ideas without copying or inventing evidence
paragraphs: Source-based writing transforms selected ideas into the required form and purpose. Paraphrase accurately, connect related points and explain their relevance to the reader. A long copied passage does not by itself show that you have interpreted the material.

Development can add a reasonable explanation or a clearly signalled proposal. It should not present an invented statistic, quotation or event as evidence from the sources. Distinguish what the sources establish from what you recommend.

example.question: Original source: “Several students cannot stay after lessons because the last bus leaves at four.” Develop this for a proposal about study support.
steps: The source identifies a transport constraint affecting some students.
Recommend a lunchtime option or accessible alternative, explaining how it addresses that constraint.
Do not invent a survey percentage or claim every student takes that bus.
example.explanation: A reasoned proposal can develop the idea while preserving the stated evidence.

commonMistakes: Attributing a new suggestion to the source writer.

sections.title: Shape an article around a clear angle
paragraphs: An article for a magazine or newspaper should give its audience a clear reason to engage with the topic. A relevant headline and focused opening can establish an angle; the main paragraphs develop connected ideas rather than repeating the headline in different words.

Use a voice appropriate to the publication and reader. Examples, contrasts or carefully chosen questions may help, but no device is compulsory in every paragraph. End by drawing the ideas together or giving an appropriate next step, rather than adding an unrelated slogan.

example.question: Write a possible original opening for an article about improving a shared study room.
steps: “A study room should make concentration easier, yet our quietest desks sit beside the busiest doorway.”
This establishes a concrete problem and a clear angle.
The next paragraph can explain a practical change and its benefit.
example.explanation: The opening leads into an argument; it is not an official model answer or guaranteed mark band.

commonMistakes: Using a headline with no developed article beneath it.
Forcing dramatic devices into a straightforward informative purpose.

sections.title: Write a speech that an audience can follow
paragraphs: A speech or talk is written for listeners. Establish why the issue matters to them, organise the argument in manageable stages and make connections clear. Direct address and deliberate repetition can support emphasis when they fit the purpose.

Rhetorical questions need an answer or a meaningful role in the argument. A list of questions and exclamations is not a developed speech. The ending can return to the central idea and give a realistic action or conclusion appropriate to the listeners.

example.question: Improve the original outline “The room is bad. Do something. Thank you.”
steps: Identify a specific problem affecting the listeners.
Explain a feasible improvement and the benefit.
End with a clear request, such as contributing ideas to a proposed trial.
example.explanation: Listeners need a chain of reasons, not only an emotional demand.

commonMistakes: Assuming every speech must be aggressive or very informal.
Adding “Dear Sir” to a task addressed to classmates as a speech.

sections.title: Match a letter to its recipient and purpose
paragraphs: A letter should make its purpose and relationship to the recipient clear. A formal request generally needs a respectful, precise opening, developed reasons and a specific desired outcome. A personal letter may use a different voice while still remaining organised and accurate.

Use appropriate greeting and closing conventions, but do not devote most of the response to addresses and layout. In an assessment, the main work is the communicated content. If personal details are not supplied, do not treat invented addresses or names as required evidence.

example.question: Original task: write to a library manager asking for a quieter study area. What makes the request useful?
steps: Explain the difficulty with a specific relevant example.
Suggest a feasible quieter area or trial arrangement.
State the action requested courteously and clearly.
example.explanation: A clear request allows the recipient to understand and respond to the proposal.

commonMistakes: Using an insulting tone when the purpose is a constructive request.
Writing only a greeting and a list of complaints.

sections.title: Write a useful contribution for its online audience
paragraphs: A contribution to a website is still sustained writing for a stated audience and purpose. A clear opening and helpful subheadings can organise a longer contribution. Paragraphs should develop ideas; the response need not become a collection of short slogans because its location is digital.

Choose language for the intended site and reader. An advice page, community argument and personal account have different needs. Do not assume that every website contribution is a casual social-media comment or requires links, buttons or a designed screen.

example.question: Plan an original website contribution offering advice about a shared study space.
steps: Open with the practical problem readers face.
Group advice under useful topics, such as noise, seating and shared responsibilities.
Explain why each suggestion helps rather than listing unexplained rules.
example.explanation: The organisation serves readers looking for understandable advice.

commonMistakes: Substituting interface design for the writing task.
Using unexplained bullet fragments throughout a sustained response.

sections.title: Plan, draft and check all three demands
paragraphs: A brief plan can record the task, a few relevant source ideas and the order in which to develop them. Group related points and decide how each paragraph advances the purpose. During drafting, keep the audience and form visible in your choices.

Review the response in passes: first task fulfilment and accurate use of sources, then sequence and development, then spelling, grammar and punctuation. A fixed checklist supports revision but does not replace whole-response judgement. Longer source-based tasks and calibrated level decisions remain necessary practice.

example.question: A draft is accurate about the sources but addresses a different audience. What should revision target?
steps: Keep the accurate source meaning.
Change explanations, register and direct address for the named audience.
Check that the required form and purpose are now sustained.
example.explanation: Accuracy in one demand does not automatically satisfy the others.

commonMistakes: Counting paragraphs as an automatic marks formula.
Proofreading spelling while leaving the task misunderstood.
